data_label: simulated data (physics model, 100 trials per point)
stats: cast iron 100 m, 20 dB, +-5% speed error
PE, 150 m spacing: fixes within 5 m

alt: Top: a 100 m pipe with two sensors, true leak at 37 m (red) and estimated position (green). Bottom: correlation function with a clear peak at the delay.
post:
A leak in a buried water main often never shows at the surface. The classic way to find a leak under the road is to listen to the pipe at two points and ask: when did the same hiss arrive at each end?

I built an open-source version of that idea in Python. It simulates a leak with the wave speed taken from pipe material and wall thickness, frequency-dependent attenuation, traffic and pump noise and sensor clock offset, then locates it with cross-correlation, GCC-PHAT and SCOT weighting. It extends to a small pipe network, adds night-noise screening, and defines a 10-byte LoRaWAN payload with raw snippets on request.

Measured in simulation: median error 0.5 m on a 100 m cast-iron span at 20 dB source SNR with up to 5% wave-speed error, 2.7 ms per correlation on a laptop CPU, and on a 9-node network 86 % of leaks assigned to the correct pipe. On PE pipe at 150 m spacing only 30 % of fixes land within 5 m, because plastic eats the signal.

Not verified: everything here is synthetic. The attenuation numbers are assumptions, and there is no real field recording, dispersion or reflection model yet.

If you have worked with leak correlators in the field: which effect hurts accuracy most in practice, wave-speed uncertainty or noise?

Code: https://github.com/Usernamepersonperson/leak-noise-correlator
